body:
My dad died last week.

Lesley and I were already in Portugal when it happened, traveling with our friends Brenda and Deb.

Dad was in hospice, but we thought we still had more time.  We always think we have more time.

In the days before we left, [**Lesley Bachleitner Hazleton**](https://www.facebook.com/lesley.b.hazleton), [**Marlis Hazleton**](https://www.facebook.com/marlis.hazleton), [**Ian Hazleton**](https://www.facebook.com/ian.hazleton.5), [**Berit Hazleton**](https://www.facebook.com/berit.hazleton), and I all had opportunities to visit Dad and say goodbye.  Ok, I did not say goodbye; I said I  love you and see you later. . . .

When Lesley told him about our planned trip to Portugal, he was very clear: Do NOT miss this trip on account of me.

So we went.

And then Dad died.

I’ve struggled with whether I should continue posting pictures and stories from Portugal.  I want to be back in Texas with Mom and my sister [**Franci Hazleton**](https://www.facebook.com/fhazleton) and the rest of my family. But I’ve realized that continuing this trip—and sharing it—is one of the most appropriate ways I can honor my dad.

Because Dad gave me the world.

When I was in second grade, our family lived in Amman, Jordan. Later we moved from Texas to Seattle, Washington. We traveled through Europe. Dad introduced me to Greece. We had a family Christmas trip where we  DROVE from Texas through Mexico all the way to Acapulco.

When Dad was at the University of Texas at Austin, we spent summers camping on some land he bought outside Nederland, Colorado.  It was the journey and stories we shared and loved to recount to anyone who would listen.

As my kids grew older, Mom and Dad took the family to the Caribbean and Greece.

My dad had a PhD in economics from Rice, but one of the most important lessons he taught me had nothing to do with a classroom:

The world is one of the best educations you can get. Go see it.

Dad gave me wanderlust.

And I’ve tried to give that same gift to my children.

As Marlis, Ian and Berit were growing up, Lesley and I took them around the United States and to Europe whenever we could.

We lived in Poland, and the United Kingdom introduced them to our friends [**Ian L Peck**](https://www.facebook.com/ian.l.peck), [**Alan Taylor**](https://www.facebook.com/alan.taylor.7798), [**Jo Peck**](https://www.facebook.com/jo.peck.35) in England and Scotland.

I wanted them to experience that same feeling Dad gave me—the realization that the world is enormous, interesting, complicated, and worth exploring.

Anyone who has followed me on Facebook knows that when I travel, I post. A LOT.

For years, a big reason I did that was Mom and Dad. They could follow along with our adventures, see where we were that day, what we’d discovered, and what ridiculous thing had inevitably happened along the way.

So I’m going to keep posting from Portugal.

There will be beautiful buildings, food, wine, bad jokes, too many pictures, and probably more information about Portuguese history than anyone asked for.

But they’ll mean something different to me now.

Every new city I walk through reminds me that Dad taught me to be curious about what was around the next corner. Every unfamiliar place reminds me that he taught me not to be afraid to go somewhere I’d never been before. And every experience I share with Lesley and our friends reminds me what an extraordinary gift that has been.

A few nights ago in Portugal, our friends gathered, and we made Manhattans with Gentleman Jack and port—a Portugal Manhattan—and raised our glasses to Jared.

Years ago, when Dad’s good friend George Douglas died, Dad and Wade Clifton opened a bottle of 12-year-old Balvenie DoubleWood and toasted George.

It seemed fitting.

So these Portugal posts are for you now, Dad.

You told me to go.

You taught me why to go.

And I promise I’ll keep going.

More importantly, I’ve tried to make sure your grandchildren will too. [**Marlis Hazleton**](https://www.facebook.com/marlis.hazleton), [**Ian Hazleton**](https://www.facebook.com/ian.hazleton.5), and [**Berit Hazleton**](https://www.facebook.com/berit.hazleton) are the best of what Dad has taught me, and I see him in them every day.

I love you, Dad.

Safe travels.

relationshipToJared: Mark's Spouse, daugher in law to Jared Hazleton
body:
Our family is grieving.  We lost my father-in-law, [**Jared Hazleton**](https://www.facebook.com/jared.hazleton), on September 3rd.  Sometimes words can be a struggle as you go through complex emotions.  There is also the complexities of the in-law relationship as it differs from a relationship with a parent.  Jared understood me in a way many in the family did not.

He was a staunch supporter of my children and loved them all unconditionally.  He challenged them, debated with them, taught them and loved them through each step of their childhood as only a grandpa can.  He shared his love of books, passion about learning and his adventurous heart with each in a different way.  He loved his grand children.

He was a father to 3 children that were as different from each other as mine are.  He gave [**Franci Hazleton**](https://www.facebook.com/fhazleton), [**Alan Hazleton**](https://www.facebook.com/alan.hazleton) and [**Mark Hazleton**](https://www.facebook.com/mark.hazleton) the support he thought they needed to succeed.  He was very proud of the family he and [**Elaine Hazleton**](https://www.facebook.com/elaine.hazleton) created.

To me, Jared was a father-in-law that worked to understand me.  He supported Mark and I when we moved the family all over creation.  He actually visitedbus at every home we lived in, even Lodz, Poland.  He supported my independence and never asked why when Mark and I made decisions for our family.  When Elaine was first diagnosed with cancer and they moved across the street, he would occasionally call and ask if we had room for an old man for dinner.  He would hang out with the kids and relax a bit before he went home to deal with harder things.

I have struggled with what to say about my father-in-law, Jared.  I have read each recounting of memories from my family and I can now sum it up.  He loved us and supported us with his actions.  He was the pillar of his family and we will miss him.  I now have lost 2 father's and that leaves another shadow across my heart.

Last night my granddad Jared Hazleton passed away. He was a loving man who I thought his grandchildren could do anything.

I've been thinking about all my memories of him and how much he loved listening to any updates about your life, he wanted to know about the clubs I was in from rugby to YDSA. He made me proud to have strong political stances even when we disagreed on them.

It also reminds me of my only solo trip with my grandfather to rapid city. it was early fall of 2020 and my grandfather wanted to take me on a college visit like he had with my sister, but because of the pandemic the only school I had planned a visit to was south Dakota School of mines. So he took me there, and we had a wonderful time. From just having more time to speak with him to him taking me to a roof top bar in South Dakota and having oyster.

I will always remember my grandfather. I hope even now I can use his memory as confidence that someone always believed I could do it and that I had followed good reason.

May he rest in peace, I will miss him dearly

relationshipToJared: Child of Mark Hazleton, Jared's Grand Child (they/them)
body:
At 5:00 pm today on September 3rd, 2026, my grandfather, [**Jared Hazleton**](https://www.facebook.com/jared.hazleton), passed away surrounded by family. This picture is from 2019, when I was lucky enough to go on a cruise with my Grandfather, my grandmother, and my aunt Franci. It’s one of my favorite memories, spending an entire week on the ocean with him. I remember when we took this photo, we have just gotten off the ship and we’re waiting for a car to pick us up and take us around Jamaica. I suprised him with the phone up, asking for a photo while we waited. It’s one of the only photos I have of the two of us.

My grandfather was an amazing man. He was smart and quick witted. When I lived in Texas, he taught me how to play chess, though I am still absolutely horrid at it. My relationship with him was intellectually debates and terrible jokes (mostly from me). He always asked about my life, and was so supportive of my love of theatre.

I am so grateful that I got to see him this past weekend. That I got to say goodbye. Our last conversation was him wishing me luck with my show, of him telling me that he was proud of me, and saying that he hopes the Rangers get to the playoffs.

I will hold the last three days I spent with him close and I will never forget the time I got to spend with him.

Rest in peace Grandpa. I already miss you so much.

relationshipToJared: Child of Mark and Lesley, Grand Child of Jared (she/her)
body:
The first year BLM began marching, Grandpa Jared asked me what I thought about them. The ensuing debate (read borderline screaming match) had to be shut down my mother who said we were being too loud and our argument had evacuated the lake house.

When I was 13 years old, Grandpa Jared asked me if I could go anywhere in the world where would I go. I was obsessed with Percy Jackson, so it was an easy choice: Greece.

And so that November we all went to Athens, Greece and I got to learn a seemingly endless amount of knowledge about Greek Mythology and the culture that created it.

I spent almost every lunch my junior year at the Conservatory eating lunch with my grandparents.

My grandpa was the first person to tell me he was proud I was a teacher (but I would be an amazing lawyer). In fact one of the last things he said to me was “I am happy you found something you love doing.”

All these memories are cycling through my mind as I try to come to terms that he is gone. That he will never see me with my masters, never see me get married.

Like my brother said in his post, Grandpa was always proud of us and I will always hold that with me. My grandfather encouraged me to be the loud, outspoken, and strong woman I am now.

I love you Grandpa, rest in peace.
